n:
*Study note:* The meaning of the *thirtieth year* is problematic. Some take it to mean the age of Ezekiel when he prophesied (e.g., Origen). The Aramaic Targum explains the thirtieth year as the thirtieth year dated from the recovery of the book of the Torah in the temple in Jerusalem ({{2 Kings 22:3|2 Kgs 22:3-9}}). The number seems somehow to be equated with the fifth year of Jehoiachin’s exile in {{Ezekiel 1:2|1:2}}, i.e., 593 b.c.

*Study note:* The Assyrians started the tactic of deportation, the large-scale forced displacement of conquered populations, in order to stifle rebellions. The task of uniting groups of deportees, gaining freedom from one’s overlords, and returning to retake one’s own country would be considerably more complicated than living in one’s homeland and waiting for an opportune moment to drive out the enemy’s soldiers. The Babylonians adopted this practice also, after defeating the Assyrians. The Babylonians deported Judeans on three occasions. The practice of deportation was reversed by the Persian conquerors of Babylon, who gained favor from their subjects by allowing them to return to their homeland. As polytheists, the Persians sought the favor of the gods of the various countries that had come under their control.

*Study note:* The *Kebar River* is mentioned in Babylonian texts from the city of Nippur in the fifth century b.c. It provided artificial irrigation from the Euphrates.

*Study note:* For the concept of the *heavens opened* in later literature, see 3 Macc 6:18; *2 Bar*. 22:1; *T. Levi* 5:1; {{Matthew 3:16|Matt 3:16}}; {{Acts 7:56|Acts 7:56}}; Rev 19:11.

*Translator's note:* Or “saw visions from God.” References to divine visions occur also in {{Ezekiel 8:3|Ezek 8:3}} and {{Ezekiel 40:2|40:2}}.

*Study note:* The prophet’s name, *Ezekiel*, means in Hebrew “May God strengthen.”

*Translator's note:* Or “to Ezekiel son of Buzi the priest.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Chaldeans.” The name of the tribal group ruling Babylon, “Chaldeans” is used as metonymy for the whole empire of Babylon. The Babylonians worked with the Medes to destroy the Assyrian Empire near the end of the 7th century b.c. Then, over the next century, the Babylonians dominated the West Semitic states (such as Phoenicia, Aram, Moab, Edom, and Judah in the modern countries of Syria, Lebanon, Jordan, and Israel) and made incursions into Egypt.

*Translator's note:* Or “power.”

*Study note:* *Hand* in the OT can refer metaphorically to power, authority, or influence. In Ezekiel God’s “hand” being on the prophet is regularly associated with communication or a vision from God ({{Ezekiel 3:14|3:14}}, {{Ezekiel 3:22|22}}; {{Ezekiel 8:1|8:1}}; {{Ezekiel 37:1|37:1}}; {{Ezekiel 40:1|40:1}}).

*Translator's note:* The word הִנֵּה (hinneh, traditionally “behold”) indicates becoming aware of something and has been translated here as a verb.

*Study note:* Storms are often associated with appearances of God (see Nah 1:3; {{Psalm 18:12|Ps 18:12}}). In some passages, the “storm” (סְעָרָה, seʿarah) may be a whirlwind ({{Job 38:1|Job 38:1}}; {{2 Kings 2:1|2 Kgs 2:1}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “fire taking hold of itself,” perhaps repeatedly. The phrase occurs elsewhere only in {{Exodus 9:24|Exod 9:24}} in association with a hailstorm. The LXX interprets the phrase as fire flashing like lightning, but it is possibly a self-sustaining blaze of divine origin. The LXX also reverses the order of the descriptors, i.e., “light went around it, and fire flashed like lightning within it.”

*Translator's note:* Or “radiance.” The term also occurs in {{Ezekiel 1:27|1:27b}}.

*Text-critical note:* Or “was in it”; cf. LXX ἐν τῷ μέσῳ αὐτοῦ (en tō mesō autou, “in its midst”).

*Translator's note:* The LXX translates חַשְׁמַל (khashmal) with the word ἤλεκτρον (ēlektron, “electrum”; so NAB), an alloy of silver and gold, perhaps envisioning a comparison to the glow of molten metal.

*Text-critical note:* *Heb* “from its midst” (מִתּוֹכָהּ, mitokhah). The LXX reads ἐν τῷ μέσῳ (en tō mesō, “in the midst of it”). The LXX also reads ἐν for מִתּוֹךְ (mitokh) in v. {{Ezekiel 1:4|4}}. The translator of the LXX of Ezekiel either read בְּתוֹךְ (betokh, “within”) in his Hebrew exemplar or could not imagine how מִתּוֹךְ could make sense and so chose to use ἐν. The Hebrew would be understood by adding “*from its midst emerged* the forms of four living beings.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “form, figure, appearance.”

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew term is feminine plural, yet thirty-three of the forty-five pronominal suffixes and verbal references that refer to the living beings in the chapter are masculine plural. The grammatical vacillation between masculine and feminine plurals suggests the difficulty Ezekiel had in penning these words as he was overcome by the vision of God. In ancient Near-Eastern sculpture very similar images of part-human, part-animal creatures serve as throne and sky bearers. For a discussion of ancient Near-Eastern parallels, see L. C. Allen, *Ezekiel* (WBC), 1:26-31. Ezekiel’s vision is an example of contextualization, where God accommodates his self-revelation to cultural expectations and norms.

*Study note:* *They had human form* may mean they stood erect.
*Study note:* The Hebrew verb translated *gleamed* occurs only here in the OT.
*Text-critical note:* The MT reads “his hand” while many Hebrew mss as well as the *Qere* read “hands of.” Two similar Hebrew letters, vav and yod, have been confused.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “They each went in the direction of one of his faces.”

*Text-critical note:* The MT has an additional word at the beginning of v. {{Ezekiel 1:11|11}}, וּפְנֵיהֶם (ufenehem, “and their faces”), which is missing from the LXX. As the rest of the verse only applies to wings, “their faces” would have to somehow be understood in the previous clause. But this would be very awkward and is doubly problematic since “their faces” are already introduced as the topic at the beginning of v. {{Ezekiel 1:10|10}}. The Hebrew scribe appears to have copied the phrase “and their faces and their wings” from v. {{Ezekiel 1:8|8}}, where it introduces the content of {{Ezekiel 1:9|9-11}}. Only “and (as for) their wings” belongs here.

*Translator's note:* See the note on “straight ahead” in v. {{Ezekiel 1:9|9}}.

*Translator's note:* Or “wind.”

*Text-critical note:* The MT reads: “and the form of the creatures” (וּדְמוּת הַחַיּוֹת, udemut hakhayyot). The LXX reads: “and in the midst of the creatures,” suggesting an underlying Hebrew text of וּמִתּוֹךְ הַחַיּוֹת (umittokh hakhayyot). The subsequent description of something moving among the creatures supports the LXX.

*Text-critical note:* The MT reads: “and the form of the creatures—their appearance was like burning coals of fire.” The LXX reads: “in the midst of the creatures was a sight like burning coals of fire.” The MT may have adjusted “appearance” to “their appearance” to fit their reading of the beginning of the verse (see the note on “in the middle”). See M. Greenberg, *Ezekiel* (AB), 1:46.

*Study note:* *Burning coals of fire* are also a part of David’s poetic description of God’s appearance (see {{2 Samuel 22:9|2 Sam 22:9}}, {{2 Samuel 22:13|13}}; {{Psalm 18:8|Ps 18:8}}).

*Text-critical note:* The LXX omits v. {{Ezekiel 1:14|14}} and may well be correct. The verse may be a later explanatory gloss of the end of v. {{Ezekiel 1:13|13}} which was copied into the main text. See M. Greenberg, *Ezekiel* (AB), 1:46.

*Translator's note:* Lit., “like the appearance of lightning.” The Hebrew term translated “lightning” occurs only here in the OT. In postbiblical Hebrew the term refers to a lightning flash.

*Text-critical note:* The MT includes “at the living beings,” which is absent from the LXX.

*Study note:* Another vision that includes *wheels* on thrones occurs in Dan 7:9. {{Ezekiel 10|Ezekiel 10}} contains a vision similar to this one.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew word may be translated either “earth” or “ground” in this context.

*Text-critical note:* This word is omitted from the LXX.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Tarshish stone.” The meaning of this term is uncertain. The term has also been translated “topaz” (NEB, NIV11), “beryl” (KJV, NASB, NRSV), or “chrysolite” (RSV, NIV84).

*Translator's note:* Or “like a wheel at right angles to another wheel.” Some envision concentric wheels here, while others propose “a globe-like structure in which two wheels stand at right angles” (L. C. Allen, *Ezekiel* [WBC], 1:33-34). The description given in v. {{Ezekiel 1:17|17}} favors the latter idea.

*Text-critical note:* The MT reads וְיִרְאָה לָהֶם (veyirʾah lahem, “and fear belonged to them”). In a similar vision in {{Ezekiel 10:12|10:12}} the wheels are described as having spokes (יְדֵיהֶם, yedehem). That parallel would suggest יָדוֹת (yadot) here (written יָדֹת without the *mater lectionis*). By positing both a ד/ר (dalet/resh) confusion and a ה/ת (hey/tav) confusion, the form was read as וְיָרֵה (veyareh) and was then misunderstood and subsequently written as וְיִרְאָה (veyirʾah) in the MT. The reading וְיִרְאָה does not seem to fit the context well, though in English it can be made to sound as if it does. See W. H. Brownlee, *{{Ezekiel 1|Ezekiel 1-19}}* (WBC), 8-9. The LXX reads καὶ εἶδον αὐτά (kai eidon auta, “and I saw”), which assumes וָאֵרֶא (vaʾereʾ). The existing consonants of the MT may also be read as “it was visible to them.”

*Translator's note:* Or “wind”; the same Hebrew word can be translated as either “wind” or “spirit,” depending on the context.

*Text-critical note:* The MT includes the additional phrase “the spirit would go,” which seems unduly redundant here and may be dittographic.

*Translator's note:* Or “wind.” The Hebrew is difficult since the text presents four creatures and then talks about “the spirit” (singular) of “the living being” (singular). According to M. Greenberg (*Ezekiel* [AB], 1:45) the Targum interprets this as “will.” Greenberg views this as the spirit of the one enthroned above the creatures, but one would not expect the article when the one enthroned has not yet been introduced.

*Text-critical note:* The LXX reads: “when it went, they went; when it stood, they stood.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “when they went, they went; when they stood, they stood.”

*Translator's note:* Or “like a dome” (NCV, NRSV, TEV).

*Translator's note:* Or “like crystal” (NRSV, NLT).

*Text-critical note:* *Heb* “each had two wings covering and each had two wings covering,” a case of dittography. On the analogy of v. {{Ezekiel 1:11|11}} and the support of the LXX, which reads the same for v. {{Ezekiel 1:11|11}} and this verse, one should perhaps read “each had two wings touching another being and each had two wings covering.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Shaddai” (probably meaning “one of the mountain”), a title that depicts God as the sovereign ruler of the world who dispenses justice. The Old Greek translation omitted the phrase “voice of the Sovereign One.”

*Translator's note:* The only other occurrence of the Hebrew word translated “tumult” is in Jer 11:16. It indicates a noise like that of the turmoil of a military camp or the sound of an army on the march.

*Text-critical note:* The MT continues: “when they stood still, they lowered their wings,” an apparent dittography from the end of v. {{Ezekiel 1:24|24}}. The LXX commits haplography by homoioteleuton, leaving out vv. {{Ezekiel 1:25|25b}} and {{Ezekiel 1:26|26a}} by skipping from רֹאשָׁם (roʾsham, “their head”) in v. {{Ezekiel 1:25|25}} to רֹאשָׁם in v. {{Ezekiel 1:26|26}}.

*Translator's note:* See {{Ezekiel 1:4|Ezek 1:4}}.

*Text-critical note:* The LXX lacks this phrase. Its absence from the LXX may be explained as a case of haplography resulting from homoioteleuton, skipping from כְּמַרְאֵה (kemarʾeh) to מִמַּרְאֵה (mimmarʾeh). On the other hand, the LXX presents a much more balanced verse structure when it is recognized that the final words of this verse belong in the next sentence.

*Study note:* Reference to the *glowing substance* and the *brilliant light* and storm phenomena in vv. {{Ezekiel 1:27|27-28a}} echoes in reverse order the occurrence of these phenomena in v. {{Ezekiel 1:4|4}}.

*Translator's note:* The vision closes with the repetition of the verb “I saw” from the beginning of the vision in {{Ezekiel 1:4|1:4}}.

*Study note:* The phrase *son of man* occurs ninety-three times in the book of Ezekiel. It simply means “human one” and distinguishes the prophet from the nonhuman beings that are present in the world of his vision.

*Text-critical note:* The phrase “as he spoke to me” is absent from the LXX.

*Translator's note:* Or “spirit.” The NIV has “the Spirit,” but the absence of the article in the Hebrew text makes this unlikely. Elsewhere in Ezekiel the Lord’s Spirit is referred to as “the Spirit of the Lord” ({{Ezekiel 11:5|11:5}}; {{Ezekiel 37:1|37:1}}), “the Spirit of God” ({{Ezekiel 11:24|11:24}}), or “my (that is, the Lord’s) Spirit” ({{Ezekiel 36:27|36:27}}; {{Ezekiel 37:14|37:14}}; {{Ezekiel 39:29|39:29}}). Some identify the “spirit” of {{Ezekiel 2:2|2:2}} as the spirit that energized the living beings; however, that “spirit” is called “the spirit” ({{Ezekiel 1:12|1:12}}, {{Ezekiel 1:20|20}}) or “the spirit of the living beings” ({{Ezekiel 1:20|1:20-21}}; {{Ezekiel 10:17|10:17}}). Still others see the term as referring to an impersonal “spirit” of strength or courage, that is, the term may also be understood as a disposition or attitude. The Hebrew word often refers to a wind in Ezekiel ({{Ezekiel 1:4|1:4}}; {{Ezekiel 5:10|5:10}}, {{Ezekiel 5:12|12}}; {{Ezekiel 12:4|12:4}}; {{Ezekiel 13:11|13:11}}, {{Ezekiel 13:13|13}}; {{Ezekiel 17:10|17:10}}, {{Ezekiel 17:21|21}}; {{Ezekiel 19:12|19:12}}; {{Ezekiel 27:26|27:26}}; {{Ezekiel 37:9|37:9}}). In {{Ezekiel 37:5|37:5-10}} a “breath” originates in the “four winds” and is associated with the Lord’s life-giving breath (see v. {{Ezekiel 37:14|14}}). This breath enters into the dry bones and gives them life. In a similar fashion the breath of {{Ezekiel 2:2|2:2}} (see also {{Ezekiel 3:24|3:24}}) energizes paralyzed Ezekiel. Breath and wind are related. On the one hand, it is a more normal picture to think of breath rather than wind entering someone, but since wind represents an external force, it seems more likely for wind rather than breath to stand someone up (unless we should understand it as a disposition). It may be that one should envision the breath of the speaker moving like a wind to revive Ezekiel, helping him to regain his breath and invigorating him to stand. A wind also transports the prophet from one place to another ({{Ezekiel 3:12|3:12}}, {{Ezekiel 3:14|14}}; {{Ezekiel 8:3|8:3}}; {{Ezekiel 11:1|11:1}}, {{Ezekiel 11:24|24}}; {{Ezekiel 43:5|43:5}}).

*Text-critical note:* The Hebrew reads “sons of,” while the LXX reads “house,” implying the more common phrase in Ezekiel. Either could be abbreviated with the first letter ב (bet). In preparation for the characterization “house of rebellion,” in vv. {{Ezekiel 2:5|5}}, {{Ezekiel 2:6|6}}, and {{Ezekiel 2:8|8}} “house” is preferred (L. C. Allen, *Ezekiel* [WBC], 1:10 and W. Zimmerli, *Ezekiel* [Hermeneia], 2:564-65).

*Text-critical note:* *Heb* “to the rebellious nations.” The phrase “to the rebellious nations” is omitted in the LXX. Elsewhere in Ezekiel the singular word “nation” is used for Israel ({{Ezekiel 36:13|36:13-15}}; {{Ezekiel 37:22|37:22}}). Here “nations” may have the meaning of “tribes” or refer to the two nations of Israel and Judah.

*Text-critical note:* This word is omitted from the LXX.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew term used here is the strongest word available for expressing a covenant violation. The word is used in the diplomatic arena to express a treaty violation ({{2 Kings 1:1|2 Kgs 1:1}}; {{2 Kings 3:5|3:5}}, {{2 Kings 3:7|7}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “sons.” The word choice may reflect treaty idiom, where the relationship between an overlord and his subjects can be described as that of father and son.

*Text-critical note:* *Heb* “stern of face and hard of heart.” The phrases “stern of face” and “hard of heart” are lacking in the LXX.

*Translator's note:* The phrase “thus says [the Lord]” occurs 129 times in Ezekiel; the announcement is identical to the way messengers often introduced their messages ({{Genesis 32:5|Gen 32:5}}; {{Genesis 45:9|45:9}}; {{Exodus 5:10|Exod 5:10}}; {{Numbers 20:14|Num 20:14}}; {{Judges 11:15|Judg 11:15}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “they”; the phrase “And as for them” has been used in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew word implies obedience rather than mere hearing or paying attention.

*Translator's note:* This Hebrew adjective is also used to describe the Israelites in {{Numbers 17:10|Num 17:10}} (17:25 HT) and {{Isaiah 30:9|Isa 30:9}}.

*Study note:* The book of Ezekiel frequently refers to the Israelites as *a rebellious house* ({{Ezekiel 2:5|Ezek 2:5}}, {{Ezekiel 2:6|6}}, {{Ezekiel 2:8|8}}; {{Ezekiel 3:9|3:9}}, {{Ezekiel 3:26|26-27}}; {{Ezekiel 12:2|12:2-3}}, {{Ezekiel 12:9|9}}, {{Ezekiel 12:25|25}}; {{Ezekiel 17:12|17:12}}; {{Ezekiel 24:3|24:3}}).

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew term occurs only here in the OT.

*Study note:* Here *thorns* may be a figure for hostility ({{Ezekiel 28:24|Ezek 28:24}}; {{Micah 7:4|Mic 7:4}}).

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew term is found elsewhere in the OT only in {{Ezekiel 28:24|Ezek 28:24}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “of their faces.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “on the face.”

*Study note:* *Written on the front and back*. While it was common for papyrus scrolls to have writing on both sides, the same was not true for leather scrolls.

*Text-critical note:* *Heb* “I ate,” a first common singular preterite plus paragogic he (ה). The ancient versions read “I ate it,” which is certainly the meaning in the context, and indicates they read the he as a third feminine singular pronominal suffix. The Masoretes typically wrote a mappiq in the he for the pronominal suffix but apparently missed this one.

*Study note:* *I ate it*. A similar idea of consuming God’s word is found in Jer 15:16 and Rev 10:10, where it is also compared to honey and may be specifically reminiscent of this text.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “deep of lip” (in the sense of incomprehensible).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “heavy of tongue.” Similar language occurs in {{Exodus 4:10|Exod 4:10}} and {{Isaiah 33:19|Isa 33:19}}.

*Translator's note:* The conjunction “but” is not in the Hebrew text but is implied from the context.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “hear.”

*Text-critical note:* The MT reads: “if not,” but most ancient versions translate only “if.” The expression occurs with this sense in {{Isaiah 5:9|Isa 5:9}} and {{Isaiah 14:24|14:24}}. See also {{Ezekiel 34:8|Ezek 34:8}}; {{Ezekiel 36:5|36:5}}; {{Ezekiel 38:19|38:19}}.

*Study note:* Moses ({{Exodus 3:19|Exod 3:19}}) and Isaiah ({{Isaiah 6:9|Isa 6:9-10}}) were also told that their messages would not be received.

*Study note:* A similar description of Israel’s disobedience is given in {{1 Samuel 8:7|1 Sam 8:7}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “hard of forehead and stiff of heart.”

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew term translated “diamond” is parallel to “iron” in Jer 17:1. The Hebrew uses two terms which are both translated at times as “flint,” but here one is clearly harder than the other. The translation “diamond” attempts to reflect this distinction in English.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “of their faces.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to the sons of your people.”

*Study note:* See note on “wind” in {{Ezekiel 2:2|2:2}}.

*Text-critical note:* This translation accepts the emendation suggested in *BHS* of בְּרוּם (berum, “in the lifting”) for בָּרוּךְ (barukh). The letters mem (מ) and kaf (כ) were easily confused in the old script, while בָּרוּךְ (“blessed be”) implies a quotation, which is out of place here. The word also does not fit the later phrase “from its place,” which requires a verb of motion.

*Translator's note:* The traditional interpretation is that Ezekiel embarked on his mission with bitterness and anger, either reflecting God’s attitude toward the sinful people or his own feelings about having to carry out such an unpleasant task. L. C. Allen (*Ezekiel* [WBC], 1:13) takes “bitterly” as a misplaced marginal note and understands the following word, normally translated “anger,” in the sense of fervor or passion. He translates, “I was passionately moved” (p. 4). Another option is to take the word translated “bitterly” as a verb meaning “strengthened” (attested in Ugaritic). See G. R. Driver, *Canaanite Myths and Legends*, 152.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the hand of the Lord was on me heavily.” The “hand of the Lord” is a metaphor for his power or influence; the modifier conveys intensity.

*Study note:* In Ezekiel God’s “hand” being on the prophet is regularly associated with communication or a vision from God ({{Ezekiel 1:3|1:3}}; {{Ezekiel 3:14|3:14}}, {{Ezekiel 3:22|22}}; {{Ezekiel 8:1|8:1}}; {{Ezekiel 37:1|37:1}}; {{Ezekiel 40:1|40:1}}).

*Study note:* The name “Tel Abib” is a transliteration of an Akkadian term meaning “mound of the flood,” i.e., an ancient mound. It is not to be confused with the modern city of Tel Aviv in Israel.

*Translator's note:* Or “canal.”

*Study note:* A similar response to a divine encounter is found in {{Acts 9:8|Acts 9:8-9}}.
*Translator's note:* The literal role of a watchman is described in {{2 Samuel 18:24|2 Sam 18:24}} and {{2 Kings 9:17|2 Kgs 9:17}}.

*Study note:* Even though the infinitive absolute is used to emphasize the warning, the warning is still implicitly conditional, as the following context makes clear.

*Translator's note:* Or “in his punishment.” The phrase “in/for [a person’s] iniquity” occurs fourteen times in Ezekiel: here and v. {{Ezekiel 3:19|19}}; {{Ezekiel 4:17|4:17}}; {{Ezekiel 7:13|7:13}}, {{Ezekiel 7:16|16}}; {{Ezekiel 18:17|18:17}}, {{Ezekiel 18:18|18}}, {{Ezekiel 18:19|19}}, {{Ezekiel 18:20|20}}; {{Ezekiel 24:23|24:23}}; {{Ezekiel 33:6|33:6}}, {{Ezekiel 33:8|8}}, {{Ezekiel 33:9|9}}; {{Ezekiel 39:23|39:23}}. The Hebrew word for “iniquity” may also mean the “punishment for iniquity.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “his blood I will seek from your hand.” The expression “seek blood from the hand” is equivalent to requiring the death penalty ({{2 Samuel 4:11|2 Sam 4:11-12}}).
*Translator's note:* Or “stumbling block.” The Hebrew term refers to an obstacle in the road in Lev 19:14.

*Translator's note:* Or “power.”

*Study note:* *Hand* in the OT can refer metaphorically to power, authority, or influence. In Ezekiel God’s *hand* being on the prophet is regularly associated with communication or a vision from God ({{Ezekiel 1:3|1:3}}; {{Ezekiel 3:14|3:14}}, {{Ezekiel 3:22|22}}; {{Ezekiel 8:1|8:1}}; {{Ezekiel 37:1|37:1}}; {{Ezekiel 40:1|40:1}}).

*Study note:* Ezekiel had another vision at this location, recounted in {{Ezekiel 37|Ezek 37}}.

*Translator's note:* See the note on “wind” in {{Ezekiel 2:2|2:2}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “you will not be to them a reprover.” In {{Isaiah 29:21|Isa 29:21}} and {{Amos 5:10|Amos 5:10}} “a reprover” issued rebuke at the city gate.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “open your mouth.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the listener will listen, and the refuser will refuse.” Because the word for listening can also mean obeying, the nuance may be that the obedient will listen, or that the one who listens will obey. Also, although the verbs are not jussive as pointed in the MT, some translate them with a volitive sense: “the one who listens—let that one listen, the one who refuses—let that one refuse.”

*Study note:* Ancient Near Eastern bricks were 10 to 24 inches long and 6 to 13½ inches wide.

*Translator's note:* Or perhaps “draw.”

*Translator's note:* Or “a barricade.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “set camps against it.”

*Translator's note:* Or “a griddle,” that is, some sort of plate for cooking.

*Translator's note:* That is, a symbolic object lesson.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I have assigned for you that the years of their iniquity be the number of days.” {{Numbers 14:33|Num 14:33-34}} is an example of the reverse, where the days were converted into years, the number of days spying out the land becoming the number of years of the wilderness wanderings.

*Text-critical note:* The LXX reads “190 days.”

*Study note:* The significance of the number 390 is not clear. The best explanation is that “days” are used figuratively for years and the number refers to the years of the sinfulness of Israel during the period of the First Temple. Some understand the number to refer to the length of the division of the northern and southern kingdoms down to the fall of Jerusalem (931-586 b.c.), but this adds up to only 345 years.

*Translator's note:* Or “When you have carried the iniquity of the house of Israel,” and continuing on to the next verse.

*Study note:* The number 40 may refer in general to the period of Judah’s exile, indicating the number of years Israel was punished in the wilderness. In this case, however, one would need to translate, “you will bear the punishment of the house of Judah.”
*Study note:* The action surely refers to a series of daily acts rather than to a continuous period.

*Study note:* *Wheat, barley, beans, lentils, millet, and spelt*. All these foods were common in Mesopotamia where Ezekiel was exiled.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “bread.”

*Text-critical note:* The LXX reads: “190 days.”

The practice of these laws and statutes would make the peoples consider Israel wise. (See {{Deuteronomy 4:5|Deut 4:5-8}}, where the words for laws and statutes are the same as those used here). Since Israel did not obey, they are made a different kind of object lesson to the nations, not by their obedience but in their punishment, as told in {{Ezekiel 5:8|Ezek 5:8}} and {{Deuteronomy 29:24|Deut 29:24-29}}. Yet {{Deuteronomy 30|Deut 30}} goes on to say that when they remember the cursings and blessings of the covenant and repent, God will restore them from the nations to which they have been scattered.

*Translator's note:* The word גִּלּוּלִים (gillulim) refers to idols with contempt. Thirty-nine of its forty-eight biblical occurrences are found in Ezekiel. It may be related to either of two roots (גלל; gll). The more common root (1-גלל) is concerned with rolling and round things, producing words like “wheel,” “bowl,” “skull,” “heap of stones,” and “dung.” The other root (2-גלל) means “to be soiled.” A possible cognate in Babylonian (gullultu) refers to a “misdeed, crime, sin” (CAD G, 131; see also gullulu, “to sin”). The pejorative use of the term may come from one of several possibilities. The basic cylindrical shape of many idols lends itself to a term from 1-גלל. As a pejorative it may be emphasizing that idols are simply blocks of wood (cf. {{Isaiah 44:19|Isa 44:19}}). It has also been suggested that the term plays off of the word for dung, גֵּל (gel), as little round things. Possibly it is related to 2-גלל with overtones of being soiled. Some relation to the Babylonian word would also suit a pejorative and may have been intended by Ezekiel as he prophesied in a Babylonian context. In any case the word carries a negative connotation.

By Ezekiel’s day the people had forgotten that the Lord (Yahweh) was their covenant God and had turned to other gods. They had to be reminded that Yahweh alone deserved to be worshiped because only he possessed the power to meet their needs. Through judgment and eventually deliverance, Israel would be reminded that Yahweh alone held their destiny in his hands.
